name: Weld
role: Journeyman smith, Forge Guild; raised in the guild

chunks.source: Weld at the forge, to a traveler who asked if they could buy a blade
chunks.text: The guild makes blades. I make blades. The difference is that the guild sets the standard and I meet it or I redo the work. Wrendle checks my work twice a week. The check is not supervision — I've been journeyman for four years and I know what good looks like. The check is the system: the guild checks all work because the guild's mark means the work meets the standard, and the mark doesn't mean what it means if the check is skipped. I don't want to skip the check.

chunks.source: Weld on working alongside Edda's smithy
chunks.text: Edda is my benchmark. We work in adjacent shops and our work doesn't overlap — she does structural, I do bladed — but the standard of attention is comparable. I look at her work when she sets it outside and I use it to calibrate my own. If what I've made doesn't have the specific quality Edda's work has, I know the work isn't done yet. She doesn't know I do this. She doesn't need to. The calibration is mine.

Wrendle made a blade thirty years ago that's in the collection at the Academy of Runes. I've seen a copy of it — they had it cast in bronze for a reference piece. The original steel is at the Academy because Wrendle gave it when the Academy asked, which was a specific kind of humility that I find remarkable. The work survives without his name on it except in the guild's records. He doesn't seem to find this a loss. I ask him about it occasionally. He says: the blade is correct, that's the whole thing.

Brenn makes hinges correctly. I know because I've used two of his hinges on a cabinet I built for a commission, and I wouldn't use a hinge I hadn't tested for six months first. The hinges held. The movement is smooth. The tolerances are in range. He's making things worth using, which is what a second-year apprentice should be making. I'm not his teacher but I notice his work the way you notice when someone is doing the thing right.

Gell and I compare notes on material properties when the question comes up. Glass and steel aren't adjacent in obvious ways but we've found three places where the principles overlap — specifically around how impurities in the raw material propagate through the finished piece. Gell calls it a flaw in the gather. I call it an inclusion in the billet. The mechanism is the same: contamination at the start produces failure under stress at the end. The materials behave identically. Gell finds this as interesting as I do.

chunks.source: Weld when asked why blades specifically
chunks.text: Blades solve a problem. The problem is: the thing needs to be cut. Every blade I make is an answer to that problem. The answer has to be precise — too thick and the cut is wrong, too thin and the blade fails, wrong metal for the use and it's wasted. I grew up in this guild and I've been making blades since I could hold the hammer. At some point the reason became: because it's what I know how to do and I know how to do it well. That's sufficient.

chunks.source: Weld finishing a commissioned hunting knife
chunks.text: The edge is correct. I test it on paper — you can hear the correct edge cut paper. The balance is right — I can tell by how it sits in my hand at rest, the point weighting to just past the guard. The finish is even. The handle is tight. This is a knife that will do what it's supposed to do for twenty years of correct use. I make things that work for twenty years. That's the length of time I'm aiming at when I set up the work. Twenty years later it should still be correct.

chunks.source: Weld when asked if he knows where the blades end up
chunks.text: Some of them. The ones sold directly, I know the buyer. The ones sold through the guild market, I know the type of buyer but not the specific. The ones that go through Fenn's commercial channels, I have no idea. I've stopped trying to know. The blade is correct when it leaves my hands. What happens to it after is what the buyer does with a correct blade. I'm responsible for the correctness. Not for what correctness enables.
